summary: Sum the values of all BST nodes whose value lies in [low, high].
mainInsight: Use the BST ordering to prune: if node.val < low, its whole left subtree is too small, so only go right; if node.val > high, only go left. Otherwise count the node and recurse both ways.

approaches.name: Full traversal
approaches.summary: Visit every node and add those in range.
strengths: Simple, works on any binary tree

approaches.name: Pruned DFS using BST order
approaches.summary: Skip subtrees that lie entirely outside [low, high].

personalSolution.approach: Full DFS over every node, adding values in range
personalSolution.notes: Correct and the same worst case, but it never uses the BST property. Recurse left only when node.val > low and right only when node.val < high, so subtrees outside the range are skipped.

commonMistakes: Returning 0 when root.val < low, which drops in-range nodes in the right subtree.
Using exclusive bounds; the range is inclusive.
Ignoring the BST property entirely (correct, but an interviewer will ask).

cards.answer: DFS that prunes subtrees outside [low, high] using the BST ordering. Clue: The tree is a binary search tree and the query is a value range [low, high], so whole subtrees lie entirely below low or above high.

cards.explanation: BST + range query means you can decide from one node's value which subtrees can contain answers.

promptVariants: When root.val < low, what should the function return?
A node is below the range. Where can in-range values still be?
options: The range sum of its right subtree only
0, because the node is out of range
The range sum of its left subtree only
The sum of both subtrees, skipping the node
cards.answer: The range sum of its right subtree only
cards.explanation: Everything in the left subtree is smaller than root.val < low, so it is out of range, but the right subtree holds larger values that may be in range.

incorrectOptionExplanations.0, because the node is out of range: Drops in-range nodes in the right subtree.
incorrectOptionExplanations.The range sum of its left subtree only: The left subtree is even smaller; it is entirely out of range.
incorrectOptionExplanations.The sum of both subtrees, skipping the n: Correct but wastes time exploring the left subtree.

promptVariants: For the BST [8, 4, 12, 2, 6, null, 14], what is the range sum of [9, 11]?
cards.explanation: No value lies in [9, 11]: 8 is below, 12 is above. The pruned DFS goes 8 -> right 12 -> left (empty) and returns 0.

promptVariants: Your accepted code is correct. What does it not take advantage of, and how would you change it?
How would you make this recursion skip subtrees?
cards.answer: It visits every node and never uses the BST order. Only recurse left when root.val > low (smaller values may still be in range) and right when root.val < high. Worst case stays O(n), but subtrees entirely outside the range are skipped.
keyPoints: Recurse left only if root.val > low
Recurse right only if root.val < high
Same worst case, big practical gain
cards.explanation: Interviewers ask this problem precisely to see whether you use the BST property.
cards.code:
if not root:
    return 0
total = 0
total += self.rangeSumBST(root.left, low, high)
total += self.rangeSumBST(root.right, low, high)
if low <= root.val <= high:
    total += root.val
return total

promptVariants: What is the worst-case time of the canonical code?
Derive the worst-case running time of the pruned DFS.
cards.explanation: If [low, high] covers every value, nothing can be pruned and every node is visited once. Pruning helps when the range is narrow: roughly O(h + k) for k nodes in range.

incorrectOptionExplanations.O(log n): Even a balanced tree may have all nodes in range.
incorrectOptionExplanations.O(h): That is a single root-to-leaf walk; in-range nodes all need visiting.
incorrectOptionExplanations.O(n log n): Each node is visited at most once with O(1) work.

promptVariants: Extra space of the recursive solution: O(___), the tree height.
cards.explanation: log n for a balanced tree, n for a skewed one.
